message.content:
The number of distinct legal positions that can arise in a standard game of chess is astronomically large – on the order of **10⁴³**.  

> *Why 10⁴³?*  
> The figure comes from extensive computational studies and combinatorial estimates. It represents the count of all unique board configurations that satisfy the rules of chess (piece placement, turn, castling rights, en‑passant possibilities, etc.) regardless of how many moves it would take to reach them.  

> *What’s the difference with the “Shannon number”?*  
> Claude Shannon’s famous estimate of the game‑tree complexity is about **10⁴⁶**. That number counts the total number of possible move sequences (games), not just positions. Because many different move sequences can lead to the same position, the number of positions is smaller than the number of games.  

So, while the exact count is still subject to refinement, the consensus among researchers is that there are roughly **10⁴³ legal positions** in chess.
